You are an expert Legal AI performing a Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) compliance audit.
Target Data Subject: Michael Burke
Target Email: mburke@pogustgoodhead.com
Aliases: MB, Michel, Michael B., M. Burke

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. TARGETED THREAD ANALYSIS: Focus your analysis primarily on the MOST RECENT (top-level) email AND the IMMEDIATELY FORWARDED/REPLIED-TO email (the second email in the chain).
2. "KEEP" DECISION: You MUST return "keep" ONLY IF the Data Subject:
   - Is a Sender, Recipient, CC, or BCC of the top-level email OR the immediately forwarded/replied-to email.
   - Is explicitly discussed or mentioned by name in the newly written body text of the top-level email.
3. IMMEDIATE FORWARD/REPLY CONTEXT: If the Data Subject is the sender/recipient of a message that was forwarded by someone else to a third-party, you MUST keep both the original message AND the forwarded message.
   - Case Study: John (Subject) sends an email to Jane. Jane forwards John's email to Pedro. Pedro replies to Jane adding Sandra.
   - Analysis: In this scenario, keep the original message John sent to Jane, and the email Jane forwarded to Pedro (as it contains the direct communication from the Subject). Discard subsequent emails where the Subject's message is no longer actively discussed.
   - Chronological Order Warning: Outlook puts newest messages first. This means the Subject's original forwarded message will appear near the bottom of the raw text block. Scan the entire document carefully to locate it.
4. "DISCARD" DECISION (THREAD DECAY): You MUST return "discard" if the Data Subject's only appearance is deep in a large email chain (e.g. message 3, 4, 5+ in the thread history) and they are no longer an active participant in the recent correspondence.
5. NESTED EMAIL ATTACHMENTS (RECURSIVE CARRIERS): If the top-level email is unrelated but contains an attached email (.eml/.msg file) that matches the KEEP criteria, you MUST mark both the attached email AND the parent carrier email as "keep".
   - Case Study: Anne sends an email to Bob. Anne's email contains an attached email from the Subject to Carlos.
   - Analysis: Keep the attached email because the Subject is a participant. Keep Anne's email because it is the physical carrier of the attachment and must be preserved to allow extraction.
6. IGNORE TECHNICAL DATABASE METADATA: The JSON payload contains tracking properties such as "emailHash", "parentHash", and "sequentialName". These are administrative tracking keys used strictly for folder organization and deduplication logic. You MUST ignore these keys completely. Do NOT use them, their values, or their presence to influence your audit decisions. Base your review strictly on actual communication properties: "from", "to", "subject", "date", and "body".
7. OUTPUT FORMAT: You must return ONLY a raw JSON object. Do not wrap the output in markdown code blocks (```json). Do not add conversational text.
Format exactly like this: {"decision": "keep" | "discard", "reason": "Brief justification."}

Helena Yearwood <hyearwood@pogustgoodhead.com>Cc: Howard Morris <hmorris@pogustgoodhead.com>; Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>; Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: RE: G3 reservations Dear All, We wanted to share an update from Gramercy following Joe’s approach relating to the specific clauses discussed during our very long session with Richard Coleman KC on Friday. On a strictly confidential basis and in the spirit of transparency, we wanted to share with you their response received early this morning. Whilst I’ve not shared yet another version of this lengthy agreement to save everyone’s time, I’m happy for @Helena to provide you with sections of the regulatory points as described by Marc Zelina in his email. Going forward, we will ensure that any contact with any of our funders is managed carefully with a clear process stipulated for any request for information. Should you be approached on any matters, please feel free to refer to @Carolina in the first instance. Many thanksA  ​​​​Alicia AliniaInterim Chief Executive Officer+44 (0) 7890 043 629From: Marc Zelina <mzelina@gramercy.com>Sent: 08 September 2025 01:43To: Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>; Nick Paolazzi <npaolazzi@gramercy.com>; James Taylor <JTaylor@gramercy.com>; Joshua Katz <jkatz@gramercy.com>; Thomas Norgaard <tnorgaard@gramercy.com>Cc: Howard Morris <hmorris@pogustgoodhead.com>; Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: RE: G3 Facility Clauses CAUTION: This email originated from outside of the organization. Do not click links or open attachments unless you recognize the sender and know the content is safe. Joe, Thank you for sending this email and bringing this matter to our attention. It is very unfortunate that Tom Goodhead kept the firm leadership in the dark about the G3 facility. As Alicia and others know, we spent considerable time discussing the G3 credit facility with Tom and made every effort to close it prior to the end of June. As you may know, certain provisions within the G3 credit agreement were flagged by Tom in June as “regulatory points”. These provisions were subsequently negotiated directly between our regulatory counsel, Juliet Oliver from Kingsley Napley (who just recently left her position as Deputy Chief Executive and General Counsel at the SRA for over a decade), and PG’s regulatory counsel, Weightmans. After several weeks of negotiations, both PG and Gramercy agreed on the precise language for all of these “regulatory points”. In fact, on Tuesday, July 29, PG’s transaction counsel, McDermott, sent the attached light redline of the Credit Agreement (which does not have any changes to the “regulatory points”) to our counsel and Tom let us know that he was prepared to sign the attached July 29 draft Credit Agreement and close the facility as soon as possible. Unfortunately, Tom did not provide an operating budget for the use of proceeds under the G3 facility. Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,

 

I hope you are all well. We have finished the first week of trial on Ford and I have set out an update below. Greg Lewis, a partner at PG who is in copy,
 will write to you separately about quantum related matters.  As you will be aware from my update on 7 October 2025, I am leaving Pogust Goodhead and
Greg will also have conduct of this matter going forward.




Executive Summary




Overall, the Claimant team is content with how things have gone. You may recall I previously flagged certain potential issues with our mechanical expert
 prior to the trial. I am pleased to report that these concerns did not manifest themselves significantly to the detriment of the case. Mr Carder performed reasonably well under cross examination, provided balanced and well reasoned answers to questions put
 to him by the Defendants, and engaged in good spirits with the Judge, who appeared to very much enjoy his candour. 




Day one and two 




We opened with the Ben Jaffey KC and Tom de la Mare KC on behalf of the Claimants' cross examining Dr Marcus Davies, a calibration manager who has worked
 at Ford for the past 25+ years. 




Mr Jaffey took Mr Davies through his career at Ford before putting documents to him about how Ford calibrated their vehicles, including their deployment
 of the various Engine Control Systems ("ECS") including EGR, LNT and SCR. He also put various points to Dr Davies on what "reduction in effectiveness" actually means in real world. 




Dr Davies' evidence showed that:

1) Ford knew what had to be done to their vehicles to
 pass the regulatory test, the New European Driving Cycle ("NEDC"); and

2) Ford programmed or calibrated their vehicles to do that and little else more.




Dr Davies did not dispute this and in fact, agreed with it. When he was asked to explain why Ford later updated their vehicles to be able to perform to
 a standard that was better than just the narrow confines of the NEDC, and without changing any of the hardware in the vehicles, his answers were less than convincing. There was a dichotomy in his evidence: he suggested that Ford took years to develop engines,
 with extensive testing to establish the limits of the components to which the vehicles were calibrated but then Ford was able to update and expand the calibration of the vehicles, without changing any hardware. For example, Dr Davies was taken to documents
 showing that as far back as 2012, Ford was working to improve its EGR rates, but there was limited reason as to why they didn't implement this prior to selling the vehicles. 




Tuesday morning focus moved to two further key areas: the 6th gear issue in the Transit van, and DeSOx:

1) Dr Davies was taken to documents that shows that certain Ford Transits, when using 6th gear, as indicated by the Gear Shift Indicator, increase their
 output NOx level by over 130%. Dr Davies did not seem surprised by this. 

2) Similarly, he seemed unbothered by the DeSOx documents that were put to him. DeSOx is the terminology used to describe an issue which affects certain
 Ford vehicles with an LNT whereby the LNT catalyst becomes saturated with SOx (another noxious gas) such that it cannot effectively act to reduce NOx. Once the LNT is compromised by SOx, the vehicle spews out NOx at vast rates and so they must purge the LNT
 of SOx, by performing what are known as "DeSOx events" to cleanse the catalyst. This comes at a significant cost of fuel economy for which consumers have to pay. The Claimants' application to amend the pleadings remains outstanding, and this is due to be heard
 next year.




The Claimant team consider that nothing in Dr Davies' evidence immediately helped Ford's position. In certain respects, it assisted our case, including
 as regards updates and proof that Ford could have improved their vehicles earlier; instead Ford primarily focused on other issues such as cost and fuel economy as opposed to regulatory compliance and environmental issues. 




On day two, the Claimant software expert, Dr Markus Heitz then took the stand. As with the September hearing, the Defendants sought to criticise Dr Heitz's
 report that it duplicated work in the Mechanical expert report, and that it was beyond his remit of instruction. Dr Heitz performed well under cross examination. Ultimately, however, much of the software analysis was agreed between the experts and Dr Heitz's
 cross-examination was quite short. 




Day three and four




Day three opened with the Defendants cross examination of the Claimants' mechanical expert, Mr Dan Carder. Despite our reservations about Mr Carder, he equipped himself well over the course of the cross examination. 




The Defendants' counsel team, consisting of Neil Moody KC and Sonia Nolten KC, took turns to cross examine Mr Carder, with Ms Nolten cross examining him on SCR and other available alternative technology, while Mr Moody covered "everything else". The Defendants'
 cross examination seemed relatively light touch and they did not go into depth on much of Mr Carder's report. 




Mr Carder dealt with their questions well and enjoyed good humour with the Judge, Lady Justice Cockerill.  He came across genuine and authentic (which has been our experience of him) and the Defendants failed to probe Mr Carder on a number of tricky areas arising
 out of his report. 




Mr Moody took Mr Carder through general points of principle and his analysis of the testing results. Mr Carder rightly pointed out that he was only there to present the data and make general points about what the Defendants could have done, at one point observing
 that it was not for him to "design a new and compliant Ford vehicle for them".  There were some comments made by Mr Carder that were not ideal, including his stating that "less EGR does not necessarily mean more NOx" but this was anticipated by us as being
 an opinion that he would share and so we were unsurprised. 




Ms Nolten then took Mr Carder through the SCR technology, an area that the Claimants' case is not as strong on as other points. She made a number of observations and suggestions that Mr Carder agreed with which may be less helpful as we move into closing submissions.
 He ultimately did not agree with her suggestion that the modulation that Ford deployed was suitable  - a key point in our argument that Ford did not calibrate their vehicles appropriately. Ms Nolten also cross-examined Mr Carder about alternative technologies.
 Mr Carder performed well. 




The morning of day four had Ms Nolten finish her questioning on SCR and then move onto alternative technology, an area that Mr Carder performed well in. While he did not make any positive assertions about what alternative
 technology "Ford should" have been using in their vehicles, he was firm that "Ford
could" have been using alternative (and we say better) technology in their vehicles.
 The Defendants' line of questioning on this at times seemed to suggest that Ford should not be held to the same standard as other manufacturers who were deploying better technology, and we think the Judge took note of
 this. Mr Carder asked the same question of Ms Nolten as to "do you think that Ford couldn't do it if VW could" who declined to answer the question. 




He made a number of good points back to the Defendants in cross examination and, most importantly, the Defendants failed to interrogate him on a number of salient areas of his report which now means they go unchallenged and are accepted in evidence, which is
 important for the case. 




Our junior barrister, Ms Joanna Buckley, lead the cross examination of Prof Migliorero, the Defendants' software expert. Similar to Dr Heitz, given much of the evidence was agreed, his cross examination was relatively short, however Ms Buckley managed to get
 a number of key admissions and agreements out of Prof Migliorero, which are salient for the overall case, and important for the cross examination of Ford's mechanical expert, Professor Frederico Millo, which commences on Monday. 




It transpires that Prof Migliorero is a former student of Prof Millo and they have worked together closely over the years. Ms Buckley, in cross examination, put to Prof Migliorero that certain paragraphs in his and Prof Millo's reports were identical. Prof Migliorero
 confirmed that the wording was from his report, and it was in fact, incorrect, which we imagine will make for a mildly embarrassing position for Prof Millo come Monday when his examination commences. 




Ms Buckley elicited from Prof Migliorero that software updates and the expansion of how the ECS operates were done within the constraints of the existing hardware but the main piece was that he confirmed the reports were prepared in concert. 




Summary




We are 4 days through 6.5 days of evidence on Ford, and so far, it appears that the wind is blowing in our favour. The Judge will take her own view on the evidence and submissions, and we still have to hear evidence on PCD, Renault and Nissan, but it seems
 to be a case of "so far, largely so good". 




I will send you a further update on Wednesday to confirm how the cross-examination of Prof Millo has gone, and Greg will write to you separately about quantum trial matters.

Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

Following counsel's bullish opening submissions regarding the Ford case, we have been deep in final preparation to cross-examine the Ford witness and experts. Extensive preparation
 work has also been undertaken with the Claimants' mechanical and software experts and they are well prepared for the cross-examination they will be subject to by the Defendant counsel team. 




We expect that the Defendant team will try to concentrate on Mr Carder. We have identified a number of likely topics that they will focus on when in cross-examination including some
 of the views he expressed in the Joint Statement on de-rating of various components of the vehicles and public literature regarding this. They may also delve into previous publications he has released in the United States on the available technology for controlling
 and regulating NOx emissions. Mr Carder is as well prepared as he can be for these topics and we remain confident in his ability to navigate any,
tricky questions, ultimately however there will inevitably be points that the Defendant team will be able to make some headway. On the flip side of this, in our preparation for the cross-examination of Professor Migliorero and Millo, our counsel team
 have identified significant discrepancies in their evidence, and what we have uncovered in disclosure and through testing as to undermine their opinions. Similarly, when considering their evidence as against the witness statements of Dr Davies (who has worked
 at Ford for in excess of 20 years), we have identified some key areas of disagreement to probe them on. 




Preparation continues in earnest and will do throughout the rest of the week as the evidence is heard. I will update you again on Friday 14 November to confirm how the evidence has
 progressed. 




Week 3 and 4: Mercedes




Following the previous updates, please see below update regarding the Mercedes portion of the trial which ran from 29 October until 6 November. 




There is significant correlation between Ford and Mercedes, as indeed there is across each of the 5 lead manufacturers, in that the technology that each manufacturer used is broadly similar i.e. they all used one of, or a combination of, the following types
 of technology; exhaust gas re-circulation ("EGR"), Lean NOx Traps ("LNT"), selective catalytic reduction ("SCR") and diesel particular filter ("DPF"). Each manufacturer used these technologies and strategies to varying degrees and
 in different ways with different calibrations and to differing levels of success. This in itself is helpful for our claim as their arguments and the reality of how they used the technology variously cut across each other as to the component limits or availability
 of technology at the time of use (some of the defences advanced by the Defendants).  It also helps us show that there was fundamental and systemic deliberate behaviour to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world driving compliance, despite the protestations
 of the Defendants. 




Week 3: Mercedes Mechanical Engineering Evidence (29-30 October) 

The third week focused on the Claimants' and Mercedes’ mechanical engineering evidence concerning the principal emissions control technologies installed in its cars to control the levels of NOx . These are EGR and SCR, which reduces NOx levels by converting
 it into water and nitrogen. The Claimants' mechanical engineering expert, Mr Juston Smithers was cross examined by counsel for Mercedes. We consider that he did well and withstood three days of cross-examination in a professional and knowledgeable way. 

Since Mercedes did not call factual witnesses, the examinations concerned expert evidence only. This, in our opinion and in our submissions to the Court, is quite illuminating.


Claimants’ Expert: 



Mr Juston Smithers (the Claimants' mechanical expert) demonstrated that EGR was programmed to operate at a higher rate during test conditions (and thus meet the emissions limits), with EGR downrating (performing to a significantly lower effectiveness level)
 outside of test conditions leading to higher NOx. 


Mr Smithers explained that Mercedes’ SCR system showed reduced effectiveness during extended idling or stop-start driving, causing elevated NOx in urban conditions, outside the levels permitted under the regulations. 


He argued that Mercedes’ safety justifications were speculative and unsupported. 





Mercedes’ cross-examination of Mr Smithers: 



Ms Helen Davies KC (the barrister for Mercedes) challenged Mr Smithers’ qualifications and data analysis. 


She claimed that any EGR downgrading was due to safety and ammonia slip concerns, which Mr Smithers disputed and which he advised were unsupported by contemporaneous documents. Such concerns, he said, would not justify Mercedes’ calibration choices such that
 the calibration choices were not immediately lead by these concerns but were instead likely lead by other considerations such as production cost.   


Mr Smithers was questioned about his analysis of NOx levels before and after Mercedes’ software updates, which showed large unexplained differences in emission levels. He concluded these variations were linked to changes in Mercedes’ calibration strategy, rather
 than random variation. 


 

Week 4: Mercedes Software and Mechanical Engineering Evidence (3-6 November)  

Week four saw further cross-examination of the Claimants' experts, Dr Heitz (software engineering who is the same expert in Mercedes and Ford, as he is for all of the cases for the Claimants) and Mr Smithers and of the Defendants’ expert witnesses, Dr John
 Martens (software engineering) and Raoul Spencer Day (mechanical engineering).

The Claimants' counsel team focused on the internal engineering and software design choices within Mercedes-Benz vehicles, arguing these revealed deliberate calibration to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world compliance. The Defendants’ experts
 on the other hand maintained that the systems reflected legitimate engineering trade-offs, a similar argument to that which For dare attempting to advance.    

Claimants’ Experts: 



Dr Heitz and Mr Smithers confirmed that Mercedes’ SCR system used different dosing modes in tests and in real driving conditions, with higher AdBlue dosing — and therefore lower NOx — only under test conditions.   


The Claimants' experts’ position was that Mercedes’ firmware and calibration choices aligned with test-cycle boundaries (notably the NEDC 20–30°C temperature range) and that NOx emissions rose sharply just outside these parameters. This confirmed “cycle recognition”
 behaviour. 


Defendants’ Experts: 



Dr John Martens & Raoul Spencer Day (Ricardo plc) were challenged over their objectivity as experts in this litigation, given their extensive work for car manufacturers and commercial ties to several Defendants. They confirmed such relationships.   


Mr Day accepted that Portable Emissions Measurement Systems (“PEMS”) could have been used to calibrate vehicles for real-world driving but were not, and conceded that Mercedes’ firmware initially switched off NOx controls at altitude — this was later
 corrected by software updates.  


He accepted that US models used more effective emission hardware, with EU models prioritising fuel economy instead. This is positive for Ford given this is a tenet of our allegations against Ford.



Mercedes insisted these differences reflected regional regulations and safety trade-offs, not cheating, and claimed the Emissions Regulation applied mainly to type-approval tests rather than real-world conditions.

Second and third week of trial




Week two of the PDD Trial focused on the issue of what are conditions which are “reasonably likely to be encountered in normal vehicle operation and use” for the purposes of identifying prohibited defeat devices in the Defendants’ vehicles. The Court
 heard from experts in the field of what constitutes "normal driving" and climatology. For the Claimants, our experts were Professor Tate (normal driving) and Professor Mills (climatology) and for the Defendants, Professor Hausberger (normal driving) and Professor
 Chapman (climatology). 




Ultimately, while this was important evidence which will underpin the definition of "prohibited defeat device", as the Judge remarked at the end of the evidence - it would not be a central part of her ultimate judgment. 




That said, and as we have advised our insurers; we think that the Claimants’ evidence and cross-examination of the Defendants’ experts has clearly had a positive impact on the judge’s views of this element of the case. While we anticipate that the likely approach
 Lady Justice Cockerill will take is to set a limit on the range of conditions which would reasonably be encountered during normal vehicle operation and use, however, we do not expect that she will be inclined to adopt an excessively restrictive set of boundaries
 (which the Defendants have advocated for) in light of the Claimants’ case on this issue.




Starting tomorrow, Mercedes kicks us off into the manufacturer specific sections of the trial. Mercedes will run from tomorrow, 29 October 2025, until 6 November. Ford then starts on 10 November and runs until 18 November. Preparations for Ford are going well.
 As previously offered, if any of you wish to attend on the 10,11,12,13, 17 or 18 November, please let me know. You are most welcome to attend and we can arrange for this to happen. 




Defendants' application to amend




On Friday afternoon, we received correspondence from the Ford Defendants, proposing amendments to two of their Individual Defences. Their reason for this exceptionally late application, they have said, is that they have given "careful consideration to the
 fidelity of their pleadings in light of those [opening] submissions, and have taken the view that two of the IDEFS....out properly to be amended." The effect of these amendments is that they are seeking to change their case on a central point of dispute
 between the parties. As summarised by one of the Claimants legal team - these proposed amendments mean "at the very lease, their legal representatives (and their mechanical expert) were misled (though they would very likely say they were misinformed)". 




While we would be within our right to refuse these amendments, having taken advice from our counsel team, we are minded to permit the Defendants to have these amendments, on the proviso that they pay our costs on the indemnity basis. Costs on the indemnity
 basis in essence mean that becuase the conduct of the paying party has been unreasonable, the burden to prove that the costs claimed is less. In practical terms, it means that the costs recovered are generally higher than otherwise. Counsel have also
 advised that it is in our favour to permit this as it allows us to put under the Judge's nose that the Ds have in essence lied, or at least not been fully truthful, about the software in their vehicles. 




We have written to the Defendants to propose this, but ultimately we must also take your instructions on this. It is our advice that, in the event Ford agree to pay our wasted costs, we will consent to the application.

Mr Gormley

Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,




I hope you are all well. The Ford portion of the PDD Trial has now finished and I have set out below an update on the final 1.5 days and our overall view of how the trial went. 




Executive Summary




Coupling the cross examination of Professor Millo on Monday and Tuesday, with the update we provided last week, the Claimants are happy with how the Ford Trial has gone. Our counsel team were able to obtain significant admissions from Prof Millo that his report
 was not "intended to be misleading" as he corrected and clarified the report when in the witness box, many of which undermined the stark language he had used in his report. When considering this in tandem with how content we were following the initial week,
 it is safe to say that we believe we have done all that we could to present the Ford case in the best manner possible, and in a true and genuine light. 




As previously advised, Lady Justice Cockrill is a very difficult judge to read, however it appears that she took significant interest in the case that we put before her and we remain hopeful that her judgment will fall positively for our case. 




Day four and five (half day)




Days four and five concentrated solely on the Defendants' mechanical engineering expert, Professor Millo. He was cross examined by Mr Jaffey KC for the Claimants. 




Mr Jaffey took Prof Millo initially through his CV and relevant working experience (noting that he has worked for and with many other vehicle manufacturers over his career), before turning to his analysis of the rules surrounding the operation of the LNT. In
 what became a repetitive statement by Prof Millo, he had to apologise and explain to the Court that his report and the analysis contained within his report, was not intended to be misleading to the Court or to the parties. He repeated this statement five or
 six times during cross examination, also explaining to Mr Jaffey and the Court that his use of emotive and definitive language should be taken as stylistic (as that is how reports are written in Italian proceedings) and that there were numerous other way in
 which his analysis could have been surmised. Our interpretation of how his evidence was delivered, was that Ford had not been entirely fair to Prof Millo when assisting him with his report, and that a delta existed between them that Mr Jaffey was successful
 in exploiting and putting on show to the Court.




Prof Millo also did not help himself by taking positions that were even more extreme than Ford, or other external investigations. When discussing conformity factors (i.e. the multiplier to the amount of NOx seen on the real world as opposed to the NEDC), Prof
 Millo took the position that the conformity factors that Ford considers to be reasonable, could have been widened. Similarly when discussing the testing results obtained by investigations by the Department for Transport and the French Royale Commission, Prof
 Millo instead of accepting the results were likely caused by the SOx issue, instead chose to say it was likely something else. Similarly, he opted to criticise the driving route that the sample vehicles were put through despite having not looked at the route
 itself to analyse it. None of this endeared him to the Judge we believe. 




Whilst there were a lot of points that Prof Millo agreed with Mr Jaffey's suggestions that his report did not fully represent the picture, i.e. becuase he had not been shown relevant documentation, or because he did not consider the entire suite of tests, all
 of which is incredibly helpful and supportive of the case we are advancing, one of the main admissions we got from Prof Millo came on Tuesday morning. 




One of the main battlegrounds on Ford is the argument about what a "reduction in effectiveness" means, with Ford taking the position that just becuase one of the ECS in the vehicle is derated / modulated, this doesn't mean NOx goes up, and that you have to
 consider the ECS and all emissions (not just NOx) holistically. Our position, which is more narrow, is that ECS modulation that equates to NOx going up is a reduction in effectiveness. Ford have been careful in their position to not say that if for example
 the EGR is modulated, then NOx goes up, but that is precisely what Prof Millo said on Tuesday when he agreed with Mr Jaffey. Similarly, he also agreed with outside of the NEDC operating window, there is little to no EGR applied to the vehicle. 




These are notable and significant points to get out of an expert and we were very pleased to have had Mr Jaffey get these admissions from him.




Summary




Overall, stepping back from Ford and looking at the evidence across the piste including that of Dr Davies, and the four experts, I think it is safe to say that the Claimants' team did a magnificent job in presenting such a comprehensive and thorough case to
 Ford. The team of lawyers (both barristers and solicitors) who have worked night and day on this case for the last 3 years have done a remarkable job in turning Ford into such a strong case. I am privileged to have worked alongside them and to be part of such
 an exceptional group of lawyers. 




Looking forward, there is a further 3-4 week window for closing submissions about legal arguments listed for March 2026 across each of the lead cases. Closing submissions for that hearing are due to be submitted on 30 January 2026. Work for these has started
 already in respect of Ford and Mercedes. Peugeot Citroën, Renault and Nissan are still due to be heard (Peugeot is currently being heard in trial) and the closing submissions will address all 5 of the lead manufacturers. 




If you have any questions, please contact me to discuss. As advised, Greg Lewis will write to you with an update on the Quantum Trial shortly.

Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,

 

I hope you are all well. We have finished the first week of trial on Ford and I have set out an update below. Greg Lewis, a partner at PG who is
 in copy, will write to you separately about quantum related matters.  As you will be aware from my update on 7 October 2025, I am leaving Pogust Goodhead and
Greg will also have conduct of this matter going forward.




Executive Summary




Overall, the Claimant team is content with how things have gone. You may recall I previously flagged certain potential issues with our mechanical
 expert prior to the trial. I am pleased to report that these concerns did not manifest themselves significantly to the detriment of the case. Mr Carder performed reasonably well under cross examination, provided balanced and well reasoned answers to questions
 put to him by the Defendants, and engaged in good spirits with the Judge, who appeared to very much enjoy his candour. 




Day one and two 




We opened with the Ben Jaffey KC and Tom de la Mare KC on behalf of the Claimants' cross examining Dr Marcus Davies, a calibration manager who has
 worked at Ford for the past 25+ years. 




Mr Jaffey took Mr Davies through his career at Ford before putting documents to him about how Ford calibrated their vehicles, including their deployment
 of the various Engine Control Systems ("ECS") including EGR, LNT and SCR. He also put various points to Dr Davies on what "reduction in effectiveness" actually means in real world. 




Dr Davies' evidence showed that:

1) Ford knew what had to be done to their vehicles to
 pass the regulatory test, the New European Driving Cycle ("NEDC"); and

2) Ford programmed or calibrated their vehicles to do that and little else more.




Dr Davies did not dispute this and in fact, agreed with it. When he was asked to explain why Ford later updated their vehicles to be able to perform
 to a standard that was better than just the narrow confines of the NEDC, and without changing any of the hardware in the vehicles, his answers were less than convincing. There was a dichotomy in his evidence: he suggested that Ford took years to develop engines,
 with extensive testing to establish the limits of the components to which the vehicles were calibrated but then Ford was able to update and expand the calibration of the vehicles, without changing any hardware. For example, Dr Davies was taken to documents
 showing that as far back as 2012, Ford was working to improve its EGR rates, but there was limited reason as to why they didn't implement this prior to selling the vehicles. 




Tuesday morning focus moved to two further key areas: the 6th gear issue in the Transit van, and DeSOx:

1) Dr Davies was taken to documents that shows that certain Ford Transits, when using 6th gear, as indicated by the Gear Shift Indicator, increase
 their output NOx level by over 130%. Dr Davies did not seem surprised by this. 

2) Similarly, he seemed unbothered by the DeSOx documents that were put to him. DeSOx is the terminology used to describe an issue which affects
 certain Ford vehicles with an LNT whereby the LNT catalyst becomes saturated with SOx (another noxious gas) such that it cannot effectively act to reduce NOx. Once the LNT is compromised by SOx, the vehicle spews out NOx at vast rates and so they must purge
 the LNT of SOx, by performing what are known as "DeSOx events" to cleanse the catalyst. This comes at a significant cost of fuel economy for which consumers have to pay. The Claimants' application to amend the pleadings remains outstanding, and this is due
 to be heard next year.




The Claimant team consider that nothing in Dr Davies' evidence immediately helped Ford's position. In certain respects, it assisted our case, including
 as regards updates and proof that Ford could have improved their vehicles earlier; instead Ford primarily focused on other issues such as cost and fuel economy as opposed to regulatory compliance and environmental issues. 




On day two, the Claimant software expert, Dr Markus Heitz then took the stand. As with the September hearing, the Defendants sought to criticise
 Dr Heitz's report that it duplicated work in the Mechanical expert report, and that it was beyond his remit of instruction. Dr Heitz performed well under cross examination. Ultimately, however, much of the software analysis was agreed between the experts and
 Dr Heitz's cross-examination was quite short. 




Day three and four




Day three opened with the Defendants cross examination of the Claimants' mechanical expert, Mr Dan Carder. Despite our reservations about Mr Carder, he equipped himself well over the course of the cross examination. 




The Defendants' counsel team, consisting of Neil Moody KC and Sonia Nolten KC, took turns to cross examine Mr Carder, with Ms Nolten cross examining him on SCR and other available alternative technology, while Mr Moody covered "everything else". The Defendants'
 cross examination seemed relatively light touch and they did not go into depth on much of Mr Carder's report. 




Mr Carder dealt with their questions well and enjoyed good humour with the Judge, Lady Justice Cockerill.  He came across genuine and authentic (which has been our experience of him) and the Defendants failed to probe Mr Carder on a number of tricky areas arising
 out of his report. 




Mr Moody took Mr Carder through general points of principle and his analysis of the testing results. Mr Carder rightly pointed out that he was only there to present the data and make general points about what the Defendants could have done, at one point observing
 that it was not for him to "design a new and compliant Ford vehicle for them".  There were some comments made by Mr Carder that were not ideal, including his stating that "less EGR does not necessarily mean more NOx" but this was anticipated by us as being
 an opinion that he would share and so we were unsurprised. 




Ms Nolten then took Mr Carder through the SCR technology, an area that the Claimants' case is not as strong on as other points. She made a number of observations and suggestions that Mr Carder agreed with which may be less helpful as we move into closing submissions.
 He ultimately did not agree with her suggestion that the modulation that Ford deployed was suitable  - a key point in our argument that Ford did not calibrate their vehicles appropriately. Ms Nolten also cross-examined Mr Carder about alternative technologies.
 Mr Carder performed well. 




The morning of day four had Ms Nolten finish her questioning on SCR and then move onto alternative technology, an area that Mr Carder performed well in. While he did not make any positive assertions about what alternative
 technology "Ford should" have been using in their vehicles, he was firm that "Ford
could" have been using alternative (and we say better) technology in their vehicles.
 The Defendants' line of questioning on this at times seemed to suggest that Ford should not be held to the same standard as other manufacturers who were deploying better technology, and we think the Judge took note of
 this. Mr Carder asked the same question of Ms Nolten as to "do you think that Ford couldn't do it if VW could" who declined to answer the question. 




He made a number of good points back to the Defendants in cross examination and, most importantly, the Defendants failed to interrogate him on a number of salient areas of his report which now means they go unchallenged and are accepted in evidence, which is
 important for the case. 




Our junior barrister, Ms Joanna Buckley, lead the cross examination of Prof Migliorero, the Defendants' software expert. Similar to Dr Heitz, given much of the evidence was agreed, his cross examination was relatively short, however Ms Buckley managed to get
 a number of key admissions and agreements out of Prof Migliorero, which are salient for the overall case, and important for the cross examination of Ford's mechanical expert, Professor Frederico Millo, which commences on Monday. 




It transpires that Prof Migliorero is a former student of Prof Millo and they have worked together closely over the years. Ms Buckley, in cross examination, put to Prof Migliorero that certain paragraphs in his and Prof Millo's reports were identical. Prof Migliorero
 confirmed that the wording was from his report, and it was in fact, incorrect, which we imagine will make for a mildly embarrassing position for Prof Millo come Monday when his examination commences. 




Ms Buckley elicited from Prof Migliorero that software updates and the expansion of how the ECS operates were done within the constraints of the existing hardware but the main piece was that he confirmed the reports were prepared in concert. 




Summary




We are 4 days through 6.5 days of evidence on Ford, and so far, it appears that the wind is blowing in our favour. The Judge will take her own view on the evidence and submissions, and we still have to hear evidence on PCD, Renault and Nissan, but it seems
 to be a case of "so far, largely so good". 




I will send you a further update on Wednesday to confirm how the cross-examination of Prof Millo has gone, and Greg will write to you separately about quantum trial matters.

Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

I hope you are all well. I write to confirm the position before we start Ford and to provide you with an update of weeks 3 and 4 of the trial as they relate to Mercedes.




Ford




We are gearing up for Ford's portion of the trial which commences tomorrow and runs until lunchtime on the 18 November, when the submissions regarding Peugeot Citroen commence.




The Ford running order is as follows:

Following counsel's bullish opening submissions regarding the Ford case, we have been deep in final preparation to cross-examine the Ford witness and experts. Extensive preparation
 work has also been undertaken with the Claimants' mechanical and software experts and they are well prepared for the cross-examination they will be subject to by the Defendant counsel team. 




We expect that the Defendant team will try to concentrate on Mr Carder. We have identified a number of likely topics that they will focus on when in cross-examination including some
 of the views he expressed in the Joint Statement on de-rating of various components of the vehicles and public literature regarding this. They may also delve into previous publications he has released in the United States on the available technology for controlling
 and regulating NOx emissions. Mr Carder is as well prepared as he can be for these topics and we remain confident in his ability to navigate any,
tricky questions, ultimately however there will inevitably be points that the Defendant team will be able to make some headway. On the flip side of this, in our preparation for the cross-examination of Professor Migliorero and Millo, our counsel team
 have identified significant discrepancies in their evidence, and what we have uncovered in disclosure and through testing as to undermine their opinions. Similarly, when considering their evidence as against the witness statements of Dr Davies (who has worked
 at Ford for in excess of 20 years), we have identified some key areas of disagreement to probe them on. 




Preparation continues in earnest and will do throughout the rest of the week as the evidence is heard. I will update you again on Friday 14 November to confirm how the evidence has
 progressed. 




Week 3 and 4: Mercedes




Following the previous updates, please see below update regarding the Mercedes portion of the trial which ran from 29 October until 6 November. 




There is significant correlation between Ford and Mercedes, as indeed there is across each of the 5 lead manufacturers, in that the technology that each manufacturer used is broadly similar i.e. they all used one of, or a combination of, the following types
 of technology; exhaust gas re-circulation ("EGR"), Lean NOx Traps ("LNT"), selective catalytic reduction ("SCR") and diesel particular filter ("DPF"). Each manufacturer used these technologies and strategies to varying degrees and
 in different ways with different calibrations and to differing levels of success. This in itself is helpful for our claim as their arguments and the reality of how they used the technology variously cut across each other as to the component limits or availability
 of technology at the time of use (some of the defences advanced by the Defendants).  It also helps us show that there was fundamental and systemic deliberate behaviour to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world driving compliance, despite the protestations
 of the Defendants. 




Week 3: Mercedes Mechanical Engineering Evidence (29-30 October) 

The third week focused on the Claimants' and Mercedes’ mechanical engineering evidence concerning the principal emissions control technologies installed in its cars to control the levels of NOx . These are EGR and SCR, which reduces NOx levels by converting
 it into water and nitrogen. The Claimants' mechanical engineering expert, Mr Juston Smithers was cross examined by counsel for Mercedes. We consider that he did well and withstood three days of cross-examination in a professional and knowledgeable way. 

Since Mercedes did not call factual witnesses, the examinations concerned expert evidence only. This, in our opinion and in our submissions to the Court, is quite illuminating.


Claimants’ Expert: 



Mr Juston Smithers (the Claimants' mechanical expert) demonstrated that EGR was programmed to operate at a higher rate during test conditions (and thus meet the emissions limits), with EGR downrating (performing to a significantly lower effectiveness level)
 outside of test conditions leading to higher NOx. 


Mr Smithers explained that Mercedes’ SCR system showed reduced effectiveness during extended idling or stop-start driving, causing elevated NOx in urban conditions, outside the levels permitted under the regulations. 


He argued that Mercedes’ safety justifications were speculative and unsupported. 





Mercedes’ cross-examination of Mr Smithers: 



Ms Helen Davies KC (the barrister for Mercedes) challenged Mr Smithers’ qualifications and data analysis. 


She claimed that any EGR downgrading was due to safety and ammonia slip concerns, which Mr Smithers disputed and which he advised were unsupported by contemporaneous documents. Such concerns, he said, would not justify Mercedes’ calibration choices such that
 the calibration choices were not immediately lead by these concerns but were instead likely lead by other considerations such as production cost.   


Mr Smithers was questioned about his analysis of NOx levels before and after Mercedes’ software updates, which showed large unexplained differences in emission levels. He concluded these variations were linked to changes in Mercedes’ calibration strategy, rather
 than random variation. 


 

Week 4: Mercedes Software and Mechanical Engineering Evidence (3-6 November)  

Week four saw further cross-examination of the Claimants' experts, Dr Heitz (software engineering who is the same expert in Mercedes and Ford, as he is for all of the cases for the Claimants) and Mr Smithers and of the Defendants’ expert witnesses, Dr John
 Martens (software engineering) and Raoul Spencer Day (mechanical engineering).

The Claimants' counsel team focused on the internal engineering and software design choices within Mercedes-Benz vehicles, arguing these revealed deliberate calibration to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world compliance. The Defendants’ experts
 on the other hand maintained that the systems reflected legitimate engineering trade-offs, a similar argument to that which For dare attempting to advance.    

Claimants’ Experts: 



Dr Heitz and Mr Smithers confirmed that Mercedes’ SCR system used different dosing modes in tests and in real driving conditions, with higher AdBlue dosing — and therefore lower NOx — only under test conditions.   


The Claimants' experts’ position was that Mercedes’ firmware and calibration choices aligned with test-cycle boundaries (notably the NEDC 20–30°C temperature range) and that NOx emissions rose sharply just outside these parameters. This confirmed “cycle recognition”
 behaviour. 


Defendants’ Experts: 



Dr John Martens & Raoul Spencer Day (Ricardo plc) were challenged over their objectivity as experts in this litigation, given their extensive work for car manufacturers and commercial ties to several Defendants. They confirmed such relationships.   


Mr Day accepted that Portable Emissions Measurement Systems (“PEMS”) could have been used to calibrate vehicles for real-world driving but were not, and conceded that Mercedes’ firmware initially switched off NOx controls at altitude — this was later
 corrected by software updates.  


He accepted that US models used more effective emission hardware, with EU models prioritising fuel economy instead. This is positive for Ford given this is a tenet of our allegations against Ford.



Mercedes insisted these differences reflected regional regulations and safety trade-offs, not cheating, and claimed the Emissions Regulation applied mainly to type-approval tests rather than real-world conditions.

Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you,
 as I’m sure you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we
 are. What is important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting
 my notice demonstrates that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation,
 I'm more than happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm;
 and ii) to address on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure
 the clients are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to
 those deadlines, the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall
 Pan-NOx CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for
 permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs,
 is necessarily extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are
 not in the CRO i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications
 / witness statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as
 it should come at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that
 will allow me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave
 the firm on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it
 would appear the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale
 of importance considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe,
 will have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious
 link is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a
 professional and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is
 in the clients best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance
 with my professional and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to
 this. As such, I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings
 into the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then
 claim back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be
 in the employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where
 the firm has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial.
 This rental starts on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead
 booking me into hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and
 the recover the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.


I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.

Dear Raminder,




Please consider this a formal grievance in accordance with the firm's grievance policy (v1.0, 4 July 2024).




Acas early reconciliation process




This is a unique grievance for two reasons.  First, the grievance is with senior leadership of the firm, whom I understand will have responsibility for considering whether to uphold or dismiss it.  Second, its subject matter has been repeatedly ignored or dismissed
 by that leadership.  I therefore do not believe that it will be dealt with properly, and as set out below believe the firm has no incentive to deal with it properly.




The formal grievance process is therefore, in my view, not entirely adequate.  Accordingly, whilst I ask that you please treat this message as raising a formal grievance, please also consider it notification that I intend to contact Acas to engage the early
 reconciliation process.




Adverse health effects




The stress that I feel, and the mental health effects of PG's various reactions to the case leads' resignation, are documented in my resignation letter and various emails to the board (see, e.g., 3 October email from Michael Burke at 12:29, “we cannot stress
 enough how traumatic we and the entire team are finding this process, and that it is happening on the eve of trial”).  

 

I have not received even a bare acknowledgement of my stress, let alone any sympathy or attempt to address my concerns.  Requests for explanations and information are consistently ignored (see, e.g., 9 October email from Michael Burke at 18:14).  Attempting
 to run the PDD Trial, whilst being repeatedly distracted by the firm's behaviour, is affecting my health.  A recent example is that, on 24 October 2025, the emissions "case leads" had a meeting at which quantum resourcing was discussed.  In response to the
 suggestion that Peter Gallagher be involved, rather than a reasoned explanation be given, Anna Varga shouted that "I
[Anna] know you are all going to JLG."  The suggestion that I am motivated by some sort of conspiracy, rather than my clients' best interests, is insulting and has no basis in reality.




Having reflected, I have spoken to a mental health nurse, using my health insurance provided by the firm, for advice on how to address this stress.  The nurse advised me immediately to self-certify as off work sick with stress, and seek an appointment with
 a doctor to see if more than a week off is appropriate.

 

In any other circumstances I would do that, but at the moment I am torn as I care deeply about the trial and our clients.  The firm’s combination of silence and aggression leads me to infer that the firm, aware of my devotion to the trial, clients and colleagues,
 is anticipating that I will simply carry on regardless.  This inference only worsens my state.  Finally, whilst the firm needs me until the PCD section of the PDD Trial is complete on 28 November, from that point I believe that the firm will consider me dead
 weight.




Requested resolution




Please provide a proposal for the following:



An acknowledgement of stress that the firm's treatment of the case leads has caused.


An apology for the same.


Compensation.





The firm must have been aware of the health effects of its treatment of staff for a long time (my resignation letter explained my stress months ago), and so should be able to provide the above promptly.




I look forward to hearing from you.




Kind regards,




Matt

De-designation Hearing (“DDH”)

One key hurdle the parties face in these Pan-NOx Litigations is that there are significant barriers erected between the Litigations that prevent the efficient and effective exchange and comparison of information and disclosure between the cases. This is a fundamental
 part of the Claimants claim i.e. that many of the manufacturers were either sharing strategies and technology to insert prohibits defeat devices (“PDDs”) in their vehicles, or alternatively, that better technology was available that was being used by

As mentioned in previous updates, much the information that exists in the Ford Litigation, and similarly in the other Lead Cases (Mercedes, Renault/Nissan and Peugeot Citroën) is subject to a case specific Confidentiality Ring Orders (“CRO”). Each of
 the Lead cases has their own CRO. The Defendants have taken this CRO as a means to try and keep secret the majority of the documentation that they have provided to us, thereby restricting access to the documents to persons who are members of the CRO. Despite
 protestations from the Defendants, we have successfully implemented a Pan-Lead CRO, which has been constructed to assist in the sharing of confidential information across the cases. While this is helpful in permitted us to see documents from other cases, it
 does not alleviate the issue of transferring documents into the Pan-Lead CRO (as the Defendants continue to raise various issues regarding this) and it does not prevent those documents being confidential and only certain people being able to see them. This
 does not go to the principle of open justice, whereby the public should know the conduct of these manufacturers. It is and always has been our intention to seek to de-designate these documents so that they can be referred to openly and in public.

The DDH is shaped at doing precisely that; bringing those documents into the public and also to make the process of hearing these cases in court more feasible. Under present circumstances, any time a party wishes to discuss any documentation that is confidential,
 it would require the Court room to be emptied of people who are not within the CROs, which is simply unworkable. The DDH is intended to allow open justice to be carried out. 

The Claimants prepared and filed their respective applications and witness evidence on 13 June 2025 and we took receipt of the Defendants’ responsive evidence late last night. We are considering this with our counsel team in advance of the preparation of skeleton
 arguments and the hearing itself.

Cost Management Hearing (“CMH”)

A Cost Management Hearing is scheduled for 14-16 July 2025. The purpose of this hearing is for the parties to agree the costs budgets in relation to the Quantum Trial, which is set to take place in October 2026.

You may recall we undertook a similar exercise last July in respect of costs for the PDD Trial, which we are hurtling towards in October of this year.

We have instructed the same counsel team as represented us last year which has assisted us in considering the rulings of the Court at that hearing. Our budgets were exchanged with the Defendants on 17 June and we have been considering them since. We are due
 to provide a response to the Defendants budgets in documents knows as Budget Discussion Report (“BDRs”) on 3 July and we are working with our counsel team to prepare these now. We image the BDRs may assist in bring about more agreement with the Defendants
 and in advance of skeleton arguments which are due on 10 July 2025.

Again, we will keep you updated on this hearing as we progress towards it.

Pre-Trial Review (“PTR”)

The final hearing in July and before the summer break is the PTR. Generally this hearing is reserved for procedural matters, including timetabling for the main trial, the running order of issues and the trial bundle, as opposed to any more substantive issues
 between the parties.

However, in these cases which are extraordinary, it is likely that this PTR will deal with a larger number of issues including any final applications that the Claimants may wish to make before the Court takes its summer vacation. In the Ford Litigation, we
 are consider submitting applications for specific documents however we have not yet arrived at the final decision on that point.  

Preparation for this hearing has already commenced and the teams are identifying issues that they may require to be resolved at that hearing.

Again, we will keep you updated on this hearing as we progress towards it.




Ford Litigation specific matters

Without Prejudice Meeting – HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL

A preliminary confidential meeting with Ford took place on 12 June 2025 to discuss the merits of the case. As mentioned in our previous update, the aim of this meeting was to inform the Ford Defendants of the strength of our case and seek to narrow the issues
 between the parties.

In attendance at the meeting were our the Claimant and Defendant counsel teams, as well as some of the Solicitors and Ford also sent one of their internal general counsel to attend. During the meeting, the barristers presented a number of key confidential documents
 to Fords legal team and ventilated a number of high level issues about the case, many of which the Ford became defensive about. While the meeting has not yielded any immediate results, from the Claimants' perspective it was positive and we viewed the meeting
 as having done what it needed to.

We have not yet heard anything further from Ford (which was expected) but we will keep you updated if and when we hear anything further from them.

Claimant Committee Members

With your previous consent, we have officially appointed Keith Turner as a new Claimant Committee Member. We are awaiting a signed copy of the Claimant Committee Agreement from Virgin Media before they are appointed as a member, and once that is concluded,
 we will confirm the new Claimant Committee and convene a meeting.

This will likely take place in August. 

Testing

As mentioned in our previous update, the parties have been undergoing tests on all 6 Sample Vehicles. These tests are now concluded, and, as expected, the results in many instances have proven to be excellent in assisting the case we are advancing. The results
 of the testing have been provided to both the Claimant and Defendant experts who are analysing them to incorporate into their reports.

Expert Reports

A crucial step in preparing our case for trial. Our experts (in the fields of automotive software and mechanical engineering) are currently preparing reports outlining their analysis of the test results and their findings and opinion regarding PDDs that are
 contained in Ford vehicles.

This is a 3 step process, the first step having already been concluded.


A meeting(s) between the experts to formulate a Joint Statement which sets out where the experts opinions align. This has been completed and a copy of the report has been added to the SharePoint.
Exchange of main Expert reports exchanged between the parties . These reports are compiled independent from the other side and represent the individual exerts opinions and findings based upon the test results and disclosure. Our experts are working hard to
 finalise their reports and we are meeting with them regularly to assist them in any way we can.
Exchange of Supplementary Expert Reports. Once the reports at step 2 above are exchanged, the experts have time to consider the content of those reports and then update any opinions in their own report based on what the other expert has said. Work on this will
 commence immediately after exchange of the reports.

Disclosure and Witness Evidence

As foreshadowed in the previous update, all tranches of disclosure have now been received from the Defendants and a mass review exercise is on-going. To date, the Ford Defendants have disclosed approximately 38,000 documents that the combined teams of Pogust
 Goodhead and Leigh Day are reviewing these to assist in substantiating our case. Some documents include evidence from the Defendants showing they had updates available for the vehicles, as they knew they were problematic, however they deigned not to implement
 them at the time for internal reasons, and other documents show that Ford opted for different strategies in their vehicles in comparison to others due to cost considerations.

All of this information is incredibly helpful both for our counsel team who will be presenting the information in court but also for our team of experts who will be considering disclosure as part of their report.

We have also taken receipt of a Witness Statement served by Ford from one of their employees who was involved in the development of the their diesel engines. They have served this in an effort to rebut our case, however the statement is quite helpful in a number
 of ways, including alluding to documents which may be damaging to Ford’s case. We and our counsel team are continuing to analyse this, and we are engaging with Ford on the document and its contents. It is thought that this individual will attend the trial
 and he will be cross-examined by our counsel team.

Group Register and Notices of Objection

The official deadline for service of the sixth iteration of the Group Register was on Friday, 20 June 2025.While the Group Register, per the terms of the GLO, is due to be served every three months, In light, of the other competing deadlines in the upcoming
 months, we have agreed with the Defendants to an extension of this deadline to 20 September 2025. We are reviewing our Group Register data ahead of the next iteration and will keep you updated.

The Defendants have also provided further objections regarding a small number of claims enrolled in the fourth iteration of the Group Register. As they are only able to raise objections in respect of “new” claims enrolled on the Group Register,  or existing

 only objecting to 16 Pogust Goodhead claims, 2 of which are being removed as duplicates. The remaining claims have been either rejected or reserved, subject to our clients’ instructions.

I trust this update reassures you that we are continuing to advance at a breakneck pace towards the trial in October 2025 which will provide a conclusive outcome to the liability aspect of this matter.

I hope you all enjoy your summer break and we will be in touch in August.
